name: Chabahar Port
description: Chabahar is a port on Iran’s Gulf of Oman coast associated with trade links to Afghanistan and Central Asia. Its Shahid Beheshti terminal became the subject of a long-term India–Iran operating agreement in 2024, while subsequent sanctions and conflict complicate assessments of its operating position.

seo.title: Chabahar Port: Terminals, Regional Trade and Operating Uncertainty | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Chabahar’s Shahid Beheshti terminal, its India–Iran agreement, regional trade ambitions and unresolved operating questions.

content.heading: A maritime gateway with an inland purpose
content.content:
Chabahar lies on Iran’s southeastern coast along the Gulf of Oman. Its international significance comes partly from the trade routes it could support inland: India has pursued the port as a connection to Afghanistan and Central Asia that avoids transit through Pakistan. This geographic rationale explains why a port in Iran features prominently in Indian regional connectivity policy. It establishes a possible route, however, rather than demonstrating the commercial reliability of every onward connection. [s4]

The most clearly documented Indian involvement concerns the Shahid Beheshti terminal. In May 2024, India’s shipping ministry described the project as a bilateral connectivity initiative and presented Afghanistan and Central Asia as intended markets. Those statements explain the participating governments’ objectives; they are not evidence that the port had already become a fully integrated regional logistics hub. [s1]

content.heading: What the terminal agreement established
content.content:
India Ports Global Limited, usually abbreviated IPGL, and Iran’s Ports and Maritime Organization, or PMO, signed their long-term agreement on 13 May 2024. A subsequent parliamentary account specified a ten-year arrangement for equipping and operating the general cargo and container terminal. General cargo and containers are distinct handling categories, so descriptions of the agreement should preserve both rather than treating the entire facility as exclusively a container terminal. [s1][s2]

Funding announcements also require careful interpretation. In an answer dated 2 April 2026, India’s Ministry of External Affairs said that the country had fulfilled its contractual contribution of USD 120 million for procuring port equipment. It reported that the final tranche had been transferred in August 2025 and explained the absence of a further allocation for the following Indian financial year on that basis. This is evidence of the government’s account of its equipment funding commitment. It does not independently establish that all equipment had been installed, that every proposed infrastructure connection was complete, or that commercial operations were uninterrupted. [s3]

content.heading: Contracts, physical condition and operations
content.content:
Developments reported in July 2026 make an unqualified description of normal operations inappropriate. Scroll reported a US strike on a tower at Chabahar and separately cited India’s foreign ministry spokesperson as saying that the terminal itself had not sustained damage. The same report, citing Business Line, said the expiry of sanctions relief in April had brought Indian project activity to a halt. These are distinct propositions about different facilities and activities; a report of damage at the port should not automatically be applied to the Shahid Beheshti terminal. [s5]

Moneycontrol also reported the spokesperson’s statement that the terminal was undamaged and that discussions with stakeholders continued after the waiver expired. That statement concerns the position described in July, not a verified operational assessment for late October. [s4]

Chabahar is therefore best understood through separate questions: what the terminal contract authorizes, what equipment funding has been provided, what infrastructure is physically available, and which services are actually operating. The inspected evidence answers the first two more firmly than the last two. Its regional importance is clear as a policy objective; its service availability at the research cutoff still requires confirmation. [s1][s3][s4][s5]

name: Northern Ports
description: Iran’s northern ports connect its transport system with the Caspian Sea, an inland body of water shared with neighboring states. Anzali, Nowshahr and Amirabad are established port names, while changing water levels make environmental conditions an essential part of understanding the region’s infrastructure.

seo.title: Iran’s Northern Ports: Caspian Gateways and Environmental Constraints | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An introduction to Anzali, Nowshahr and Amirabad, their Caspian setting, and the environmental constraints affecting port infrastructure.

content.heading: Ports on an inland sea
content.content:
Iran’s northern maritime gateways face the Caspian Sea, the inland water body bordered by Iran, Azerbaijan, Kazakhstan, Russia and Turkmenistan. This setting gives them a different regional context from Iran’s southern ports. An account of northern shipping must consider conditions across the Caspian rather than assuming the operating geography of an open-ocean port. [s2]

The International Association of Ports and Harbors lists Anzali, Noshahr and Amirabad among the ports associated with Iran’s Ports and Maritime Organization, or PMO. Noshahr is another English rendering of Nowshahr. The directory also describes PMO responsibilities concerning ports, coastal facilities and maritime commerce. It establishes the ports’ institutional context, but provides neither a complete inventory of every northern facility nor a comparable account of their present cargo activities. [s1]

content.heading: A network that requires more than port capacity
content.content:
A port’s inclusion in a regional network should be distinguished from evidence of a particular scheduled service. Kazakhstan’s Aktau port maintains a partner directory that includes Amirabad and Anzali. This provides direct institutional evidence of regional port relationships, but does not establish sailing frequency, cargo volumes or guaranteed connections between the listed facilities. [s3]

OECD research on Caspian transport identifies vessel availability, adverse weather and falling water levels as constraints on maritime movements. Its detailed operating examples concern other Caspian ports, especially in Kazakhstan, and should not be transferred to Iranian facilities as if they were local measurements. The regional lesson is nevertheless relevant: a quay and storage area are only part of a functioning route. Vessel suitability and reliable access to the water also matter. [s2]

content.heading: The coast is part of the infrastructure
content.content:
The United Nations Environment Programme describes declining Caspian water levels as a concern for infrastructure, economies and ecosystems. Its working-paper abstract emphasizes that evaporation, rainfall, river discharge, water use and diversions interact, with climate change influencing these variables. This supports treating coastal change as a long-term planning issue rather than attributing it to a single cause. It does not supply a measured depth for any individual Iranian harbor. [s4]

Anzali also illustrates the close relationship between a port city and a sensitive coastal environment. The Ramsar Information Sheet locates Anzali Wetland beside Bandar Anzali in Gilan Province and describes its lagoon, marshes, rivers and importance for migratory birds and fish. It records sedimentation, pollution and Caspian water-level fluctuations among the wetland’s pressures. These findings concern the wetland; they do not by themselves establish that port operations caused each pressure. [s5]

Understanding northern ports therefore requires two kinds of evidence together: transport records showing what each facility handles, and environmental records showing the conditions in which it operates. The inspected material establishes the principal names and the importance of that environmental setting. A fuller comparison still needs port-specific cargo profiles, access depths, inland connections and consistent annual statistics.

name: Container Shipping
description: Container shipping moves cargo in standardized intermodal containers and depends on both terminal operations and shipping services. In Iran, understanding the sector requires distinguishing container throughput from vessel capacity, port performance and the availability of trade connections.

seo.title: Container Shipping in Iran: TEUs, Terminals and Performance | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Learn how container shipping is measured, why throughput differs from efficiency, and what Iran’s terminal agreements can establish.

content.heading: What a container statistic measures
content.content:
Container shipping uses standardized units that can be handled by ships and terminals. Its familiar statistical abbreviation, TEU, means twenty-foot equivalent unit. The World Bank’s port performance glossary counts a standard twenty-foot container as one TEU and a forty-foot container as two. Consequently, a figure expressed in TEUs is not simply a count of physical boxes. [s1]

The same glossary distinguishes TEUs from container moves. Loading or discharging a container counts as a move regardless of its size. This matters when comparing crane activity with container volumes: two terminals can record the same number of moves while handling different TEU totals. A ship’s nominal container capacity is another separate quantity. It describes carrying capacity, rather than how many containers a port actually handled during a year. [s1]

content.heading: Volume does not establish efficiency
content.content:
The World Bank publishes an Iran indicator for container port traffic, identifying UN Trade and Development, or UNCTAD, as its data provider. Its national geographic scope is essential: the indicator should not be presented as the traffic of an individual terminal or shipping company. An Iran-wide total cannot establish which port gained cargo or whether a particular service was available. [s2]

Operational performance requires a different lens. The World Bank’s Container Port Performance Index 2023 assesses performance using vessel time in port. Its glossary separates waiting, time alongside the berth and crane activity. These distinctions help explain why a busy port is not necessarily a fast port, and why a single annual throughput figure cannot reveal the source of delays. The index’s focus on vessels also means it should not be treated as a complete measure of a shipment’s journey beyond the terminal. [s1]

content.heading: Reading Iranian terminal announcements
content.content:
Chabahar provides a concrete example of the difference between an operating framework and a measured result. India’s shipping ministry described its May 2024 agreement with Iran as covering the equipping and operation of a general cargo and container terminal at Shahid Beheshti. The contract identifies an activity and participating institutions. It does not supply a national container traffic series or establish the availability of every onward service. [s3]

A separate Indian parliamentary answer in April 2026 reported fulfillment of the equipment funding commitment under that agreement. That is a financial and contractual statement, rather than an observation of container throughput. Keeping these categories separate prevents investment announcements from being presented as completed cargo movements. [s4]

For readers assessing Iran’s container sector, the useful questions are therefore specific: which terminal is being measured, whether the unit is TEUs or moves, which reporting period applies, and whether the figure describes actual activity or available capacity. Annual comparisons also need consistent geographic coverage. The evidence inspected here supports those distinctions, but a reconciled historical series and a verified account of services at the research cutoff remain necessary before presenting a quantitative assessment of the sector. [s1][s2][s3][s4]
